claim: In human cells, cytoplasmic dynein-1 is essential for long-distance transport of many cargos, including organelles, RNAs, proteins, and viruses, towards microtubule minus ends.
source: In human cells, cytoplasmic dynein-1 is essential for long-distance transport of many cargos, including organelles, RNAs, proteins, and viruses, towards microtubule minus ends.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about dynein function in the field.

claim: Human dynein/dynactin requires 'activators' to achieve maximal motile activity and to bind its cargos.
source: To achieve maximal motile activity and to bind its cargos, human dynein/dynactin requires 'activators', of which only five have been described.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Only five dynein activators have been described prior to this study.
source: To achieve maximal motile activity and to bind its cargos, human dynein/dynactin requires 'activators', of which only five have been described.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this work.

claim: Ninein and ninein-like are a new family of dynein activators.
source: We developed methods to identify new activators in our BioID data, and discovered that ninein and ninein-like are a new family of dynein activators.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Each dynein activator has multiple cargos.
source: Analysis of the protein interactomes for six activators, including ninein and ninein-like, suggests that each dynein activator has multiple cargos.
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data for six activators showing multiple protein interactions.

claim: Mutations in the microtubule transport machinery cause both neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Mutations in the transport machinery cause both neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases (Lipka et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The human genome contains 15 motor domain-encoding dynein genes.
source: The human genome contains 15 motor domain-encoding dynein genes (Vale, 2003), but only cytoplasmic dynein-1 (DYNC1H1; 'dynein' hereafter) is involved in long-distance, minus-end-directed transport in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vale, 2003.

claim: Only cytoplasmic dynein-1 is involved in long-distance, minus-end-directed transport in the cytoplasm.
source: The human genome contains 15 motor domain-encoding dynein genes (Vale, 2003), but only cytoplasmic dynein-1 (DYNC1H1; 'dynein' hereafter) is involved in long-distance, minus-end-directed transport in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: Dynein transports dozens of distinct cargos including organelles, ribonucleoprotein complexes, proteins and viruses.
source: Dynein transports dozens of distinct cargos including organelles, ribonucleoprotein complexes, proteins and viruses (Kardon and Vale, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Dimers of the S. cerevisiae dynein heavy chain move processively in the absence of cofactors.
source: While dimers of the S. cerevisiae dynein heavy chain move processively in the absence of cofactors (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006), mammalian dynein requires the 1.1 MDa dynactin complex and a coiled coil-containing activator ('activator' hereafter) for robust processive motility (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014; Trokter et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Reck-Peterson et al., 2006.

claim: Mammalian dynein requires the 1.1 MDa dynactin complex and a coiled coil-containing activator for robust processive motility.
source: While dimers of the S. cerevisiae dynein heavy chain move processively in the absence of cofactors (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006), mammalian dynein requires the 1.1 MDa dynactin complex and a coiled coil-containing activator ('activator' hereafter) for robust processive motility (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014; Trokter et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Activators link dynein/dynactin to cargo.
source: Activators have a second function; they also link dynein/dynactin to cargo (Figure 1A) (Cianfrocco et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: BICD2 and HOOK3 have been definitively shown to activate dynein/dynactin motility in vitro using purified components.
source: The activators BICD2 and HOOK3 have been definitively shown, using purified components, to activate dynein/dynactin motility in vitro (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014; Schroeder and Vale, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: HOOK1, Spindly (SPDL1), and RAB11FIP3 are likely activators based on their ability to co-purify and co-migrate with dynein/dynactin in in vitro motility assays.
source: HOOK1, Spindly (SPDL1), and RAB11FIP3 are also likely activators based on their ability to co-purify and co-migrate with dynein/dynactin in in vitro motility assays (McKenney et al., 2014; Olenick et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Known and predicted activators all contain long stretches of predicted coiled coil.
source: Known and predicted activators all contain long stretches of predicted coiled coil, but share very little sequence homology across activator families (Gama et al., 2017); currently it is not possible to identify activators based on sequence alone.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and is used as a basis for the screening approach.

claim: It is not currently possible to identify dynein activators based on sequence alone.
source: Known and predicted activators all contain long stretches of predicted coiled coil, but share very little sequence homology across activator families (Gama et al., 2017); currently it is not possible to identify activators based on sequence alone.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge in the field.

claim: IC2-BioID was incorporated into the dynein/dynactin complex.
source: Immunoprecipitations confirmed that IC2-BioID was incorporated into the dynein/dynactin complex (Figure 1B—E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: 51% of the BioID-tagged IC2 was incorporated into the dynein complex.
source: Gel filtration analysis of IC2 immunoprecipitates revealed that 51% of the BioID-tagged IC2 was incorporated into the dynein complex (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on gel filtration analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 47% of p62-BioID was incorporated into the high molecular weight dynactin complex.
source: gel filtration analysis of these immunoprecipitatates revealed that 47% was incorporated into the high molecular weight dynactin complex (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on gel filtration analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The IC2 BioID dataset identified all dynein subunits and a number of dynactin subunits.
source: Our IC2 BioID dataset identified all dynein subunits, as well as a number of dynactin subunits (Figure 2B—D and Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2B-D and supplementary files.

claim: The IC2 BioID dataset contained the known activators BICD2, HOOK1, and HOOK3, as well as BICD1.
source: In addition, the dataset contained the known activators BICD2, HOOK1, and HOOK3, as well as BICD1, a homolog of BICD2 that is a likely activator (Figure 2D and Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2D and supplementary files.

claim: Spindly was not identified in the IC2 BioID dataset because it regulates mitotic-specific dynein functions in human cells.
source: Spindly regulates mitotic-specific dynein functions in human cells (Chan et al., 2009; Gassmann et al., 2010), likely the reason we did not identify it in an unsynchronized cell population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of Spindly and the experimental conditions used.

claim: RAB11FIP3 is poorly expressed in HEK-293T cells.
source: RAB11FIP3 is poorly expressed in HEK-293T cells (Huttlin et al., 2015) (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and data shown in Table 1.

claim: The dynein IC is well positioned within the dynein/dynactin/activator complex for the BioID-based identification of activators.
source: These experiments show that the dynein IC is well positioned within the dynein/dynactin/activator complex for the BioID-based identification of activators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing IC2 BioID identified activators.

claim: IC1 and IC2 BioID samples detected more dynactin subunits than either LIC1 or 2.
source: IC1 and IC2 BioID samples detected more dynactin subunits than either LIC1 or 2, consistent with the dynein LIC being further away from dynactin compared to the IC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with structural studies.

claim: The IC1, LIC1 and LIC2 dynein subunits and the p62 dynactin subunit identified dynein activators.
source: With respect to activators, we found that the IC1, LIC1 and LIC2 dynein subunits and the p62 dynactin subunit identified dynein activators (Figure 3C and Supplementary files 1 and 3).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary files.

claim: BioID provides spatial information about the large dynein complex.
source: Thus, BioID provides spatial information about the large dynein complex, which is capable of moving in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing BioID can report on the spatial organization of the complex.

claim: BioID experiments with the dynein IC and LIC subunits and dynactin p62 subunit can be used to identify activators.
source: Importantly, these results also show that BioID experiments with the dynein IC and LIC subunits and dynactin p62 subunit can be used to identify activators, providing a method to discover dynein activators in other cell types or tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: All known activators contain long stretches of coiled coil.
source: Because all known activators contain long stretches of coiled coil (Figure 4B), we pooled datasets with known activators present (IC1, IC2, LIC1, LIC2, and p62) and selected a set of proteins with predicted coiled coils of at least 100 amino acids.
evidence: This is based on analysis of known activators shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A hallmark of known activators is their ability to co-immunoprecipitate dynein and dynactin.
source: A hallmark of known activators is their ability to co-immunoprecipitate dynein and dynactin (McKenney et al., 2014; Olenick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Ninein (NIN), ninein-like (NINL), daple (CCDC88C) and girdin (CCDC88A) co-immunoprecipitated dynein and dynactin.
source: Four proteins analyzed in our secondary screen, ninein (NIN), ninein-like (NINL), daple (CCDC88C) and girdin (CCDC88A), co-immunoprecipitated dynein and dynactin, as did our positive controls BICD2 and HOOK3 (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NIN was identified in the IC1 and IC2 BioID datasets.
source: NIN was identified in the IC1 and IC2 BioID datasets, NINL and daple in the IC2 BioID dataset, and girdin in the LIC1 dataset (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: NINL and daple were identified in the IC2 BioID dataset.
source: NIN was identified in the IC1 and IC2 BioID datasets, NINL and daple in the IC2 BioID dataset, and girdin in the LIC1 dataset (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Girdin was identified in the LIC1 BioID dataset.
source: NIN was identified in the IC1 and IC2 BioID datasets, NINL and daple in the IC2 BioID dataset, and girdin in the LIC1 dataset (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: BICD2 and HOOK3 exhibited robust processive motility in single-molecule motility assays.
source: Our positive controls, BICD2 and HOOK3, exhibited robust processive motility, as did NIN and NINL (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is based on single-molecule motility data shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: NIN and NINL exhibited robust processive motility in single-molecule motility assays.
source: Our positive controls, BICD2 and HOOK3, exhibited robust processive motility, as did NIN and NINL (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is based on single-molecule motility data shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: Daple and girdin showed only a very modest ability to isolate activated dynein/dynactin complexes.
source: In contrast, daple and girdin showed only a very modest ability to isolate activated dynein/dynactin complexes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is based on single-molecule motility data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: BICD2 activated and co-migrated with processively moving dynein and dynactin in reconstituted assays.
source: As expected, BICD2 activated and co-migrated with processively moving dynein and dynactin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on three-color TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NIN and NINL activated and co-migrated with moving dynein/dynactin complexes in reconstituted assays.
source: Both NIN and NINL also activated and co-migrated with moving dynein/dynactin complexes (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on three-color TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: In the absence of an activator dynein/dynactin is largely stationary, with some diffusive and rare processive runs observed.
source: In the absence of an activator dynein/dynactin is largely stationary, with some diffusive and rare processive runs observed (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on single-molecule motility data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The BioID method can identify dynein activators.
source: Together, our results show that the BioID method can identify dynein activators, including the members of a new family of activators we discovered here: NIN and NINL.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing BioID identified NIN and NINL as activators.

claim: For the known activators BICD2 and HOOK3, their N-termini interact with dynein/dynactin and their C-termini bind to cargos or cargo adaptor proteins.
source: We made both N- and C-terminal BioID fusions with each activator because, for the known activators BICD2 and HOOK3, their N-termini interact with dynein/dynactin and their C-termini bind to cargos or cargo adaptor proteins (Cianfrocco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In comparison to N-terminal datasets, the C-terminal datasets had more unique hits, more hits shared between activators, and more total hits (except for NIN).
source: Overall, in comparison to N-terminal datasets, the C-terminal datasets had more unique hits (except for NIN), more hits shared between activators, and more total hits (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Only four out of 225 proteins in N-terminal datasets were present in at least one dataset from each activator family.
source: When we performed this analysis for the N-terminal datasets only four out of 225 proteins were present in at least one dataset from each activator family (Figure 6B, white circles).
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Three of the four proteins present in all N-terminal activator family datasets were dynein subunits (HC, LIC1, and LIC2).
source: Strikingly, three of these four proteins were dynein subunits (HC, LIC1, and LIC2), highlighting that the shared function associated with the N-termini of activators is their interaction with dynein.
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 21 out of 547 proteins in C-terminal datasets were present in each activator family.
source: When we performed this analysis with the C-terminal datasets we found 21 out of 547 proteins were present in each activator family (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of the 21 proteins present in all C-terminal activator family datasets revealed an association with cellular locations that correlate with microtubule minus ends.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (Gene Ontology Consortium, 2015) of these 21 proteins revealed an association with cellular locations that correlate with microtubule minus ends ('ciliary basal body', 'microtubule organizing center', and 'centrosome') (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of BioID data shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: The BICD2 C-terminal interactome was enriched for GO terms relating to cortical actin cytoskeleton structures, including adherens junctions and focal adhesions.
source: The BICD2 C-terminal interactome was enriched for GO terms relating to cortical actin cytoskeleton structures, including adherens junctions and focal adhesions (Supplementary file 5), consistent with previous studies that have linked dynein to these cortical actin-based structures (Ligon et al., 2001; Rosse et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of BioID data shown in Supplementary file 5 and is consistent with published studies.

claim: The HOOK3 C-terminal interactome was enriched for GO terms relating to clathrin coated vesicles.
source: The HOOK3 C-terminal interactome was enriched for GO terms relating to clathrin coated vesicles (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of BioID data shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Both the NIN and NINL C-terminal interactomes were enriched for GO terms generally related to structures found at microtubule minus ends.
source: Both the NIN and NINL C-terminal interactomes were enriched for GO terms generally related to structures found at microtubule minus ends (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of BioID data shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Activators within families share significant sequence similarity.
source: Activators within families share significant sequence similarity (global identity, global similarity: BICD1/BICD2 = 53.6%, 65.2%; HOOK1/HOOK3 = 57.0%, 73.2%; NIN/NINL = 21.1%, 33.9%).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of activator proteins.

claim: Activators from the same protein family had more C-terminal-specific overlap than activators from different families.
source: Reflecting this protein conservation, activators from the same protein family had more C-terminal-specific overlap than activators from different families (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data shown in Table 2.

claim: The BICD activator family was enriched for GO terms associated with the actin cytoskeleton.
source: The BICD activator family was enriched for GO terms associated with the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of BioID data.

claim: The HOOK family was enriched for GO terms related to kinesin motors.
source: The HOOK family was enriched for GO terms related to kinesin motors (Supplementary file 5); we identified C-terminal-specific interactions of HOOK1 and HOOK3 with the kinesins KIF1C and KIF5B, as well as the KIF5B associated light chains, KLC2 and KLC4 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis and BioID data shown in Supplementary files 4 and 5.

claim: C-terminal-specific interactions of HOOK1 and HOOK3 with the kinesins KIF1C and KIF5B were identified.
source: The HOOK family was enriched for GO terms related to kinesin motors (Supplementary file 5); we identified C-terminal-specific interactions of HOOK1 and HOOK3 with the kinesins KIF1C and KIF5B, as well as the KIF5B associated light chains, KLC2 and KLC4 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: The NIN family was enriched for GO terms related to microtubule minus ends.
source: The NIN family was enriched for GO terms related to microtubule minus ends (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of BioID data shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: HOOK1 and HOOK3 are members of the FHF complex, which is involved in endosomal sorting.
source: HOOK1 and HOOK3 are members of the FHF complex, which is involved in endosomal sorting (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Proteins in the FHF complex (AKTIP/FTS and FAM160A2/FHIP) were identified as specifically enriched in the HOOK1 and HOOK3 datasets.
source: We identified proteins in this complex (AKTIP/FTS and FAM160A2/FHIP), as well as two proteins that are homologous to FAM160A2 (FAM160A1, FAM160B1) as specifically enriched in the HOOK1 and HOOK3 datasets.
evidence: This is based on BioID data analysis.

claim: FAM160A2 was reported to interact with HOOK3 and AKTIP/FTS in a recent high-throughput proteomics study.
source: FAM160A1 and FAM160A2 share sequence identity (global identity 36.4%, global similarity 50.5%), and FAM160A2 was reported to interact with HOOK3 and AKTIP/FTS in a recent high-throughput proteomics study (Huttlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RIMBP3, a known HOOK1 interacting protein involved in spermatogenesis, was identified as a HOOK1 C-terminal-specific hit.
source: We also identified RIMBP3, a known HOOK1 interacting protein involved in spermatogenesis, as a HOOK1 C-terminal-specific hit (Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on BioID data and is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RANBP2, a well-characterized BICD2-interacting protein, was identified in the BICD2 interactome.
source: In the BICD2 interactome, we identified RANBP2, a well-characterized BICD2-interacting protein that is responsible for targeting dynein/dynactin/BICD2 to nuclear pore complexes (Splinter et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on BioID data and is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The NINL C-terminal interactome was specifically enriched for MICAL3, a protein that interacts with Rab8 and is localized to the base of primary cilia in a NINL-dependent manner.
source: The NINL C-terminal interactome was specifically enriched for MICAL3, a protein that interacts with Rab8 and is localized to the base of primary cilia in a NINL-dependent manner (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on BioID data and is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The interaction of HOOK3 with KIF1C and FAM160A2/FHIP was specific to the C-terminus of HOOK3.
source: In agreement with our BioID data, immunoprecipitation experiments showed that the interaction of KIF1C and FAM160A2/FHIP with HOOK3 was specific to the C-terminus of HOOK3 (553–718) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), while dynein's interaction was specific to the N-terminus of HOOK3 (aa 1–552) (McKenney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and is supported by a citation.

claim: Dynein's interaction with HOOK3 was specific to the N-terminus of HOOK3 (aa 1–552).
source: In agreement with our BioID data, immunoprecipitation experiments showed that the interaction of KIF1C and FAM160A2/FHIP with HOOK3 was specific to the C-terminus of HOOK3 (553–718) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), while dynein's interaction was specific to the N-terminus of HOOK3 (aa 1–552) (McKenney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data and is supported by a citation to McKenney et al., 2014.

claim: HOOK3 may represent a new class of dynein activator that can also recruit the opposite polarity motor KIF1C.
source: In addition, this data suggests that HOOK3 may represent a new class of dynein activator, one that not only activates dynein/dynactin, but can also recruit the opposite polarity motor KIF1C.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the finding that HOOK3 interacts with both dynein and kinesin.

claim: BioID reports on the spatial organization of both the tripartite dynein/dynactin/activator complex, as well as the domain organization of dynein activators.
source: Our data show that BioID reports on the spatial organization of both the tripartite dynein/dynactin/activator complex, as well as the domain organization of dynein activators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Girdin and daple are candidate dynein/dynactin activators.
source: We identified ninein and ninein-like as a new family of dynein activators and two Hook-related proteins, girdin and daple, as candidate dynein/dynactin activators.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing they co-immunoprecipitate dynein/dynactin but do not conclusively activate motility.

claim: Each activator will link dynein to multiple cargos.
source: We propose that these proteins represent novel dynein cargos, cargo adaptors or regulators of motor-cargo interactions and that each activator will link dynein to multiple cargos.
evidence: This is a proposal based on analysis of activator interactomes showing multiple protein interactions.

claim: Both NIN and NINL localize to the centrosome.
source: Both NIN and NINL localize to the centrosome, are involved in microtubule nucleation, and have been shown previously to immunoprecipitate with dynein/dynactin (Casenghi et al., 2005, 2003; Delgehyr et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NIN and NINL are involved in microtubule nucleation.
source: Both NIN and NINL localize to the centrosome, are involved in microtubule nucleation, and have been shown previously to immunoprecipitate with dynein/dynactin (Casenghi et al., 2005, 2003; Delgehyr et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NIN and NINL have been shown previously to immunoprecipitate with dynein/dynactin.
source: Both NIN and NINL localize to the centrosome, are involved in microtubule nucleation, and have been shown previously to immunoprecipitate with dynein/dynactin (Casenghi et al., 2005, 2003; Delgehyr et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ability of NIN and NINL to activate dynein suggests that they control their own, as well as any associated proteins, recruitment to the centrosome or other sites of microtubule nucleation.
source: The ability of NIN and NINL to activate dynein suggests that they control their own, as well as any associated proteins, recruitment to the centrosome or other sites of microtubule nucleation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that NIN and NINL activate dynein and localize to the centrosome.

claim: NINL has been implicated in dynein-based vesicle trafficking.
source: NINL has also been implicated in dynein-based vesicle trafficking (Dona et al., 2015), in support of the idea that each activator has multiple cargos (see below).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Girdin and daple are Hook-related proteins.
source: Girdin and daple are Hook-related proteins (Simpson et al., 2005), which also act as guanine nucleotide exchange factors for small G proteins (Aznar et al., 2016, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Girdin and daple act as guanine nucleotide exchange factors for small G proteins.
source: Girdin and daple are Hook-related proteins (Simpson et al., 2005), which also act as guanine nucleotide exchange factors for small G proteins (Aznar et al., 2016, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both daple and girdin are phosphoproteins.
source: For example, both daple and girdin are phosphoproteins (Table 1) (Huttlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and data shown in Table 1.

claim: CCDC88B/gipie is related to girdin and daple and interacts with dynein and dynactin.
source: CCDC88B/gipie is related to girdin and daple and interacts with dynein and dynactin (Ham et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Gipie is not expressed in HEK-293T cells.
source: We did not identify gipie in our screen, likely because it is not expressed in HEK-293T cells (Table 1) (Huttlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and data shown in Table 1.

claim: The number of dynein activators is much smaller than the number of dynein cargos.
source: Our findings suggest that the number of dynein activators is much smaller than the number of dynein cargos, strongly implying that each activator links dynein to multiple cargos.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited number of activators identified and the known diversity of dynein cargos.

claim: BICD2 interacts with both Rab6 and RanBP2.
source: There are hints of this concept in the literature as BICD2 interacts with both Rab6 and RanBP2 (Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016), and in Drosophila the RNA binding protein egalitarian (Dienstbier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GO analysis of the interactomes of six distinct dynein activators suggests that each of these activators is involved in multiple dynein-based functions.
source: Consistent with this, our GO analysis of the interactomes of six distinct dynein activators suggests that each of these activators is involved in multiple dynein-based functions.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of BioID data.

claim: Activators provide the first layer of defining cargo specificity for cytoplasmic dynein.
source: We propose that activators provide the first layer of defining cargo specificity for cytoplasmic dynein, but that refinement of cargo selection will require additional factors.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the analysis of activator interactomes.

claim: Refinement of cargo selection will require additional factors beyond activators.
source: We propose that activators provide the first layer of defining cargo specificity for cytoplasmic dynein, but that refinement of cargo selection will require additional factors.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the analysis of activator interactomes showing multiple interactions per activator.

claim: The 1.4 MDa dynein holoenzyme is composed of dimers of heavy chains, intermediate chains, light intermediate chains, and three types of light chains.
source: The 1.4 MDa dynein holoenzyme is composed of dimers of heavy chains (HC; DYNC1H1), intermediate chains (IC1 or IC2; DYNC1I1 and 2), light intermediate chains (LIC1 or LIC2; DYNC1LI1 and 2), and three types of light chains: Roadblock (RB; DYNLRB1 and 2), LC8 (DYNLL1 and 2), and TCTEX (DYNLT1 and 3) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynein structure.

claim: BioID G2 was used for all BioID experiments in this study.
source: We first generated a cell line stably expressing IC2 with C-terminal BioID G2 ('BioID' here) (Kim et al., 2016b) and 3×FLAG tags.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: Detergent conditions used in BioID experiments disrupt both the dynein and dynactin complexes.
source: To perform BioID experiments, we lysed cells in the presence of additional detergents (see Materials and methods), which disrupt both the dynein and dynactin complexes (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: Disruption of the dynein and dynactin complexes makes it likely that BioID experiments identified only proximal proteins that were modified with biotin prior to cell lysis.
source: Disruption of the complexes makes it likely that our BioID experiments identified only proximal proteins that were modified with biotin prior to cell lysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: Hits in BioID experiments were defined as proteins with greater than 3-fold enrichment and p-values greater than 0.05 relative to the control.
source: 'Hits' were proteins with greater than 3-fold enrichment and p-values greater than 0.05 relative to the control.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis criteria used in the study.

claim: The dynein IC is centrally located within the tripartite dynein/dynactin/activator complex based on cryo-EM structural studies.
source: We first characterized the IC2 subunit of dynein, which is known to be centrally located within the tripartite dynein/dynactin/activator complex based on cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structural studies (Figure 1A) (Chowdhury et al., 2015; Urnavicius et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published cryo-EM structural studies.

claim: Spindly regulates mitotic-specific dynein functions in human cells.
source: Spindly regulates mitotic-specific dynein functions in human cells (Chan et al., 2009; Gassmann et al., 2010), likely the reason we did not identify it in an unsynchronized cell population.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The finding that IC1 and IC2 BioID samples detected more dynactin subunits than LIC1 or 2 is consistent with the dynein LIC being further away from dynactin compared to the IC.
source: IC1 and IC2 BioID samples detected more dynactin subunits than either LIC1 or 2, consistent with the dynein LIC being further away from dynactin compared to the IC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on BioID data and is consistent with structural studies.

claim: The finding that IC1, LIC1, LIC2, and p62 identified activators is consistent with the current structural model of the dynein/dynactin/activator complex.
source: This finding is consistent with the current structural model of the dynein/dynactin/activator complex (Chowdhury et al., 2015; Urnavicius et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison of BioID data with published structural studies.

claim: Prefoldin is a T-complex co-chaperone.
source: Further validation of our approach came from the presence of T-complex and prefoldin subunits as IC-specific hits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as prefoldin is a T-complex co-chaperone, and T-complex has been shown to interact with newly synthesized ICs (Özdemir et al., 2016; Vainberg et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: T-complex has been shown to interact with newly synthesized ICs.
source: Further validation of our approach came from the presence of T-complex and prefoldin subunits as IC-specific hits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as prefoldin is a T-complex co-chaperone, and T-complex has been shown to interact with newly synthesized ICs (Özdemir et al., 2016; Vainberg et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The presence of T-complex and prefoldin subunits as IC-specific hits validates the BioID approach.
source: Further validation of our approach came from the presence of T-complex and prefoldin subunits as IC-specific hits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as prefoldin is a T-complex co-chaperone, and T-complex has been shown to interact with newly synthesized ICs (Özdemir et al., 2016; Vainberg et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on BioID data and known interactions from the literature.

claim: Reconstituted purified dynein and dynactin occasionally show processive runs in the absence of an activator.
source: Because reconstituted purified dynein and dynactin occasionally show processive runs in the absence of an activator (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014), we cannot yet conclude if daple and girdin are bona fide dynein activators.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The gold standard assay for dynein activators is to reconstitute dynein/dynactin/activator motility from purified components.
source: The gold standard assay for dynein activators is to reconstitute dynein/dynactin/activator motility from purified components (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: BICD2 activated and co-migrated with processively moving dynein and dynactin in reconstituted assays with purified components.
source: As expected, BICD2 activated and co-migrated with processively moving dynein and dynactin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on three-color TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5B using purified components.

claim: NIN and NINL activated and co-migrated with moving dynein/dynactin complexes in reconstituted assays with purified components.
source: Both NIN and NINL also activated and co-migrated with moving dynein/dynactin complexes (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on three-color TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D using purified components.

claim: The shared function associated with the N-termini of activators is their interaction with dynein.
source: Strikingly, three of these four proteins were dynein subunits (HC, LIC1, and LIC2), highlighting that the shared function associated with the N-termini of activators is their interaction with dynein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from analysis of N-terminal BioID data.

claim: No dynein subunits were detected in the C-terminal activator BioID datasets.
source: In contrast to the N-terminal dataset we did not detect any dynein subunits in the C-terminal dataset.
evidence: This is based on analysis of C-terminal BioID data.

claim: BioID can report on the distinct protein interactions of different regions of the dynein activators.
source: Overall, this data highlights the power of the BioID technique to report on the distinct protein interactions of different regions of the dynein activators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of N- and C-terminal BioID data.

claim: Each activator had dozens of C-terminal specific hits.
source: Each activator had dozens of C-terminal specific hits (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary files 1 and 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary files 1 and 4.

claim: C-terminal specific hits are candidates for activator-specific cargos, cargo adaptors, or proteins that regulate how dynein connects to its cargo.
source: These proteins are candidates for activator-specific cargos, cargo adaptors, or proteins that regulate how dynein connects to its cargo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the C-terminal specific hits identified in BioID data.

claim: Previous studies have linked dynein to cortical actin-based structures including adherens junctions and focal adhesions.
source: The BICD2 C-terminal interactome was enriched for GO terms relating to cortical actin cytoskeleton structures, including adherens junctions and focal adhesions (Supplementary file 5), consistent with previous studies that have linked dynein to these cortical actin-based structures (Ligon et al., 2001; Rosse et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: FAM160A1 and FAM160A2 share sequence identity (global identity 36.4%, global similarity 50.5%).
source: FAM160A1 and FAM160A2 share sequence identity (global identity 36.4%, global similarity 50.5%), and FAM160A2 was reported to interact with HOOK3 and AKTIP/FTS in a recent high-throughput proteomics study (Huttlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: RANBP2 is responsible for targeting dynein/dynactin/BICD2 to nuclear pore complexes.
source: In the BICD2 interactome, we identified RANBP2, a well-characterized BICD2-interacting protein that is responsible for targeting dynein/dynactin/BICD2 to nuclear pore complexes (Splinter et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MICAL3 interacts with Rab8 and is localized to the base of primary cilia in a NINL-dependent manner.
source: The NINL C-terminal interactome was specifically enriched for MICAL3, a protein that interacts with Rab8 and is localized to the base of primary cilia in a NINL-dependent manner (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Studies in filamentous fungi have linked dynein, Hook, and kinesin.
source: Although Hook proteins are not known to interact with kinesins in humans, studies in filamentous fungi have linked dynein, Hook, and kinesin (Bielska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments verified the interaction of HOOK3 with the dynein heavy chain, FAM160A2/FHIP, and KIF1C.
source: We used co-immunoprecipitation experiments to verify the interaction of HOOK3 with the dynein heavy chain, FAM160A2/FHIP, and KIF1C (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: BioID data identified the interaction of HOOK3 with KIF1C and FAM160A2/FHIP as C-terminal-specific.
source: Our BioID data had identified the interaction of HOOK3 with KIF1C and FAM160A2/FHIP as C-terminal-specific and the interaction with dynein/dynactin as N-terminal-specific.
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data.

claim: BioID data identified the interaction of HOOK3 with dynein/dynactin as N-terminal-specific.
source: Our BioID data had identified the interaction of HOOK3 with KIF1C and FAM160A2/FHIP as C-terminal-specific and the interaction with dynein/dynactin as N-terminal-specific.
evidence: This is based on analysis of BioID data.

claim: Immunoprecipitation experiments validated the BioID data showing spatially restricted interactions of HOOK3.
source: This data further validates the BioID approach and highlights how BioID can identify spatially restricted interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the agreement between BioID and immunoprecipitation data.

claim: BICD2 interacts with the RNA binding protein egalitarian in Drosophila.
source: There are hints of this concept in the literature as BICD2 interacts with both Rab6 and RanBP2 (Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016), and in Drosophila the RNA binding protein egalitarian (Dienstbier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: BICD1 and BICD2 are elongated structures.
source: BICD1 and 2, the best structurally characterized dynein activators, are known to be elongated structures (Liu et al., 2013; Terawaki et al., 2015; Urnavicius et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: Other activators are likely elongated structures.
source: Given this, and the likely elongated nature of other activators, we reasoned that BioID would be ideally suited to report on the spatially separated functional differences between the N- and C-termini of activators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structure of BICD proteins and the presence of long coiled coils in other activators.

claim: HOOK proteins have been shown to heterodimerize.
source: HOOK proteins have been shown to heterodimerize (Xu et al., 2008), whereas heterodimerization between BICD proteins has not been reported.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Heterodimerization between BICD proteins has not been reported.
source: HOOK proteins have been shown to heterodimerize (Xu et al., 2008), whereas heterodimerization between BICD proteins has not been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of reports in the literature.

claim: BICD1 was identified in BICD2 datasets and vice versa.
source: We note that we identified BICD1 in our BICD2 datasets and vice versa (Supplementary files 1 and 4).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Supplementary files 1 and 4.

claim: HOOK1 was identified in HOOK3 datasets and vice versa.
source: The same was true for HOOK1 and HOOK3, but not for NIN and NINL (Supplementary files 1 and 4).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Supplementary files 1 and 4.

claim: NIN was not identified in NINL datasets and vice versa.
source: The same was true for HOOK1 and HOOK3, but not for NIN and NINL (Supplementary files 1 and 4).
evidence: This is based on BioID data shown in Supplementary files 1 and 4.
